source.title: CEAMC: Corpus and Empirical Study of Argument Analysis in Education via LLMs
source.authors: Yupei Ren; Hongyi Wu; Zhaoguang Long; Shangqing Zhao; Xinyi Zhou; Zheqin Yin; Xinlin Zhuang; Xiaopeng Bai; Man Lan

record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates downstream argument-classification performance across models and relates the results to scaling, but does not reproduce pretraining-loss or compute-allocation experiments.
record.gate_note: The paper reports argument-classification F1 results and claims they confirm scaling laws. It does not measure held-out pretraining loss, fit loss power laws, test extrapolation, or find compute-optimal allocations. Its benchmark results are included only for V6.
record.test_reason: This is an argument-mining corpus and benchmark paper. It fine-tunes and prompts heterogeneous models (BERT, RoBERTa, Longformer, three 6–7B LLMs, closed APIs) on one classification task. It then says the LLM-over-PLM gap 'confirms the scaling laws (Kaplan et al., 2020)'. It does not vary scale within a model family, does not state PLM sizes, and does not measure loss or relate scores to compute, parameters or loss. The comparison mixes architecture, pretraining data and fine-tuning method (full fine-tuning vs LoRA), so no version, including V6, is actually tested. The scaling-law remark is an interpretive citation.
record.recipe_differences: This is a downstream argument-classification benchmark using SFT, ICL, and CoT, rather than a language-model pretraining loss or compute-allocation study.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports performance differences across SFT, ICL, and CoT and across ICL shot counts; it notes that more prompt examples do not always improve results.

fits_no_version.finding: On CEAMC fine-grained classification (Table 4), LoRA-tuned 6–7B LLMs mostly beat fully fine-tuned BERT/RoBERTa/Longformer. However, RoBERTa (Macro-F1 39.87, Micro 74.43) beats ChatGLM3-6B (36.60, 69.23). The authors read the overall gap as confirming scaling laws without any scale-controlled comparison.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Cross-family comparisons of downstream task scores between small encoders and ~7B LLMs are sometimes cited as evidence for scaling laws, though they do not isolate scale.

record.peer_reviewed: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2024
record.problems: The scaling-related conclusion rests on benchmark comparisons among heterogeneous models, with only 6B and 7B sizes stated for the open-source LLMs; there is no controlled scale sweep, held-out pretraining-loss measurement, or uncertainty reporting for the relevant scores.
record.rows_left_out: ICL and CoT scores and per-category F1 results are omitted because the scaling-related comparison is made in the SFT discussion; the study does not relate those prompt-method outcomes to model scale.

untested.parts: No shape variation at fixed size.
No power-law fits in other regimes.
No controlled scale variation or loss–task relation; model sizes for PLMs and closed APIs not stated.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests/T2' with a V6 limits_scope label is overturned. There is no within-family scale variation, PLM sizes are unstated, and the fine-tuning method differs between groups (full fine-tuning vs LoRA), so the rows cannot bear on V6. The scaling-law statement is the authors' interpretation, not a test. The coarse-grained SFT results (Table 12) show the same pattern and do not change this.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute.
Prediction of larger-run losses from fits to smaller runs.
Compute-optimal parameter/token allocations and their trends with compute.
Effects of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Power-law behavior in other modalities or training regimes.
The study reports downstream task scores but does not measure pretraining loss or test predictability over a broad scale range.
Dependence of scaling fits or compute-optimal splits on setup and fitting choices.

relation.reason: Section 4.4.1 and the conclusion interpret LLM versus PLM performance as confirming scaling laws, but provide no test of predictable improvement with scale.

tranche.reason: The study benchmarks heterogeneous models on argument classification without measuring a scaling curve, pretraining loss, extrapolation or compute allocation. Its results do not establish any listed claim version.

source_check.notes: All twelve scores match Table 4 and its percentage units. The authors' scaling interpretation exceeds the evidence: model families and training conditions differ, with no scale-controlled comparison or predictive fit.
